827.title: Where you go
827.hook: Ruth to Naomi: where you go I will go
827.howItsDone: Ruth's words to Naomi are read at some weddings and conversion ceremonies, and in Jewish communities the book of Ruth is read at the festival of Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Moses, and the stranger. Your line was history carried in the body. Today, a stranger who chose to stay.

Three widows are standing on a road out of Moab. Naomi, the older one, has buried her husband and both her sons. Her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, have buried their husbands too. Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she tells the young women to turn around: "Go, return each to her mother's house." She has nothing left to give them. They cry. Orpah kisses her and goes. Ruth doesn't move. The King James puts it in a handful of words: "Ruth clave unto her."
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH KISSES HER AND GOES.` → `RUTH DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: Start with the one who leaves, because the story is kind to her. Naomi asked both women to go, and blessed them: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me." Orpah does what she was asked, and the text never scolds her. Going home was sensible, and allowed. That's what makes Ruth stand out: she had an honorable way out, and didn't take it. Look at the verb. "Ruth clave unto her" uses the same English verb the King James uses in Genesis for a man who will "cleave unto his wife." Clinging, holding on. Earlier this year came her opening words, whither thou goest. Today, the line that follows, which goes further: "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried." Ruth isn't promising a trip. She's promising a whole life, and a grave, in a country where she'll be the foreigner: yesterday's stranger, seen from the other side. She doesn't talk about how she feels; she names a direction. In Bethlehem, Ruth gleans, gathering leftover barley behind the reapers in someone else's field so the two of them can eat. Later the field's owner, Boaz, tells her: "thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning." The Hebrew behind kindness there is chesed, the steady, loyal love from the start of this block. Some readers take that sentence as the book's quiet center: love that keeps going after the moment when leaving would have been fine.
screen: `ORPAH GOES, AND NO ONE BLAMES HER.` · `RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.` · `WHERE THOU DIEST, WILL I DIE.` · `KINDNESS IN THE LATTER END.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is in a hard stretch, someone it would be easy, even reasonable, to drift away from, and picture walking beside them one more mile. You're not fixing anything, just staying; if you pray, you can hold them before God by name. Then let a quiet question rest there: what would staying look like, a call, a ride, an hour on their couch?
Ruth. The widow who left her own people to stay with Naomi, and gleaned barley in Bethlehem so the two of them could eat. Today's word.
Your line: clinging, holding on. A promise with a direction in it. Day eight hundred twenty-seven, done.

828.title: David and Jonathan
828.hook: David mourns Jonathan's love as wonderful
828.howItsDone: Readers of the Hebrew Bible point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and some keep up old friendships with letters, calls or visits on anniversaries and holidays.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ruth, the widow who stayed. Your line was clinging, holding on. Today, another kind of loyalty: two friends.

"Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women." A warrior sings that over a dead friend. The news has just reached David: King Saul and his son Jonathan have fallen in battle on Mount Gilboa. Saul has hunted David. Jonathan was Saul's son, the heir to the throne David would one day take. By the usual rules of politics, they should have been rivals. Instead, near the end of David's lament, come Jonathan's name and that line. Today: how it began, what it cost, and what came after.
screen: `THY LOVE TO ME WAS WONDERFUL.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND HIS RIVAL.` → `BEGINNING, COST, AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: It begins with a sentence that doesn't sound like politics at all. After David's victory over Goliath, "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads. Then Jonathan takes off his own robe and gives it to David, with his sword, his bow and his belt. Some readers see a prince handing over the signs of his rank. Then the friendship gets expensive. Saul wants David dead, and Jonathan, caught between his father and his friend, warns David at real risk to himself. Later he says it outright: you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. The heir steps aside in his own words. Readers have heard this bond in more than one way; the text itself calls it love and a covenant. Then, after the grief, once David is king, he asks a question nobody needed him to ask: "Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" There is: Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, living quietly far from court. David gives him back his grandfather's land and seats him at the king's table for good. Kindness here is that same Hebrew word from yesterday, chesed. The friend is gone. The friendship keeps going, as a seat at the table for his son.

segments.voice: Let an old friend come to mind, someone who once stood next to you, at school, at work, in a hard year, whom life has carried somewhere else. Remember one specific thing, a joke, a kitchen, a drive, something they did for you, and hold it for a few breaths. Let the first sentence of a note form in your head, not an apology for the silence, just the memory; if you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Covenant. The binding promise Jonathan made with David, knit together as friends even though one stood between the other and the throne. Today's word.
Your line: the friend. A covenant can outlive the one who made it. Tomorrow, a love poem.

829.title: Strong as death
829.howItsDone: Some Jewish communities read the Song of Songs in the synagogue during Passover, and lines from its eighth chapter are read at some weddings, Jewish and Christian.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was covenant, and a kindness that outlived a friend. Your line was the friend. Today, a love poem from the Bible.

A seal is a small thing: a carved stone or a ring, pressed into wax or clay, and the mark it leaves says, this is mine, this comes from me. Near the end of the Song of Songs, one lover asks to become one. Not to be given one, or to wear one: to be the seal, pressed onto the other's heart and arm. And in the same breath, the poem gives love a much bigger rival than sweetness or patience.
screen: `A SEAL: THIS IS MINE.` → `PRESSED ONTO THE HEART.` → `A MUCH BIGGER RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse in the King James: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave." First, the seal. The speaker doesn't ask to be remembered fondly. She asks to be the mark itself, on the heart where feeling lives and on the arm where work gets done: love meant to show, inside and out. Second, the comparison. Death is a force nobody bargains with, and it doesn't let go. Love, the poem says, is just as strong. And it isn't only gentle: jealousy is cruel as the grave, and its coals are "coals of fire." Third, the water. The next verse adds: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Love is the fire the floods can't put out. Fourth, how it's read. Read plainly, the Song is love poetry between two lovers, and some readers take it that way. Jewish tradition has also read it as the love between God and Israel; the Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva calling the Song the holy of holies among the scriptures. Christian readers have heard Christ and the church, or God and the soul. These readings sit side by side. Whichever you hear, the claim is bold: love isn't the soft thing in the room. It's as strong as death.
screen: `SET ME AS A SEAL.` · `STRONG AS DEATH, CRUEL AS THE GRAVE.` · `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH IT.` · `LOVERS, GOD AND ISRAEL, OR THE SOUL.` · then, large: `LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Choose one person you love and rarely tell, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, and let their face come. Find the one plain sentence you've been too shy, too busy or too cool to say: I love you, I'm proud of you, you changed my life. Say it silently a few times, slowly, until it feels less strange, and if you pray, let it become a prayer for them.
Seal. The Song of Songs' image for love: pressed onto the heart and the arm, a mark meant to show both inside and out. Today's word.
Your line: many waters cannot quench love. A fire the floods can't put out. That's day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: God is love
830.hook: a short letter answers what God is in three words
830.howItsDone: Christians read First John in worship and private prayer, and the line God is love appears on church walls, cards and gravestones.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was seal, love pressed onto the heart and the arm. Your line was many waters cannot quench love. Today, the New Testament, and a three-word sentence.

Ask a room of people what God is, and the answers get long fast. Maker of everything. Judge. Spirit. Mystery. Philosophers keep trying. Near the end of the New Testament there's a short letter, traditionally linked to the apostle John, that answers in three words. Not God has love, or God gives love, or God loves. Something stranger, and harder to get out of: God is love.
screen: `WHAT IS GOD?` → `THE ANSWERS GET LONG.` → `A LETTER ANSWERS IN THREE WORDS.`

segments.voice: In the King James, the fourth chapter of First John reads: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." First, the shape. The letter doesn't say love is one of God's qualities, the way a person is tall or patient. It says God is love, as if love were what God is made of, and Christian writers keep turning that over. Second, the problem a few verses later: "No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us." The unseen God shows up where people love each other. Third, the order: "We love him, because he first loved us." Love doesn't start with us; it's received first, then passed on. Fourth, the test, and it's blunt: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." If you can't love the brother you can see, the letter reasons, how would you love God, whom you can't? So the sentence isn't only a comfort. It's a measuring stick. Whatever else a reader believes about God, in the letter's terms love isn't proven in the sky. It's proven at the kitchen table, the office, the group chat, with the person right in front of you.
screen: `NOT GOD LOVES: GOD IS LOVE.` · `NO MAN HATH SEEN GOD.` · `WE LOVE, BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED.` · `THE TEST: THE BROTHER YOU CAN SEE.` · then, large: `GOD IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture one ordinary moment still ahead of you today, a meeting, a meal, a conversation that usually goes sideways, and the person you'll see there. Ask what acting from love would look like there, just once: not a feeling to force but an act, like listening to the end, letting them go first, saying thank you and meaning it. If you pray, rest in those three words from First John; if not, rest with the person's face.

Your line: proven at the kitchen table. Three words, with a test attached. Day eight hundred thirty, done.

831.title: Love your enemies
831.hook: love your enemies, pray for them that persecute you
831.howItsDone: Christians pray for people they find difficult, sometimes by name in private prayer, and some churches include prayers for enemies or for those who wish them harm in their regular worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was First John, the letter that says God is love. Your line was proven at the kitchen table. Today, the hardest test of that sentence.

Loving a friend is easy to admire. Loving a stranger, as this block heard a few days ago, takes some work. But there's often someone in a life who is neither: the coworker who undermined you, the relative who keeps score, the ex, the neighbor with the leaf blower and the grudge. On a mountain in Galilee, in the teaching Christians call the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus names that person directly. He doesn't say tolerate them, or avoid them, or forgive them eventually. He says something that sounds almost impossible.
screen: `A FRIEND, A STRANGER.` → `AND THE PERSON WHO HURT YOU.` → `A SERMON ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The King James puts it like this: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you," and the verse goes on: pray for those who mistreat and persecute you. First, the verbs: love, bless, do good, pray. None is a feeling you have to fake; each is something a person can do while the hurt is still there. Second, the reason. God, Jesus says, "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." The sunrise doesn't check anyone's record, and neither does the rain. To love an enemy, in this teaching, is to be a little like that: given to everyone. Third, the roots. This isn't a break with the scripture Jesus grew up with. Proverbs already says, "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat." Jesus takes up that thread and carries it on, from bread to blessing to prayer. Fourth, the Gospels show him doing it. In Luke, from the cross, he prays for the men crucifying him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Christians apply this in different ways. Some traditions, like the Mennonites and the Quakers, read it as a call to refuse violence altogether; other churches read it as a command about the heart and daily conduct that still leaves room for defending the innocent. Both take it seriously. Love here isn't approval. It's wanting good for someone who doesn't want good for you.
screen: `LOVE, BLESS, DO GOOD, PRAY.` · `SUN ON THE EVIL AND ON THE GOOD.` · `IF THINE ENEMY BE HUNGRY.` · `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Let one difficult person come to mind, not the worst one, someone you can picture without your stomach knotting completely, and let whatever rises, anger, hurt, tiredness, simply be there. Then slowly wish them one ordinary good thing: sleep tonight, a day without pain, someone who is kind to them. You don't have to mean it perfectly, and if you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Agape. The love Jesus commands even for enemies: bless them, do good to them, pray for them, like the sun that rises on everyone. Today's word.
Your line: even them. Wanting their good, without pretending the hurt away. Until tomorrow, then.

832.title: Washing feet
832.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some other churches hold a foot-washing on the Thursday before Easter, and some smaller churches wash one another's feet as part of communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agape, love even for enemies. Your line was even them. Today, love you can see, and smell, and get wet from.

A towel, a basin, some water: that's the whole scene's equipment. It's the last supper Jesus shares with his friends before his arrest, in John's Gospel, and the room is full of people who have walked dusty roads in sandals. Partway through the meal, he gets up. He takes off his outer garment, ties the towel around his waist, pours water into the basin, and kneels in front of the first pair of feet. The room goes quiet. One of them is about to object, loudly.
screen: `A TOWEL, A BASIN, SOME WATER.` → `HE GETS UP FROM SUPPER.` → `HE KNEELS AT THEIR FEET.`

segments.voice: John opens the scene with love: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then, instead of a speech, a chore. First, whose job this was. When Abigail agrees to marry David in First Samuel, she says, "let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." In her words, it's the task of a servant who serves the servants. Second, Peter. He can't stand it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers him, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, being Peter, swings the other way: then not just my feet, but my hands and my head. Letting yourself be served turns out to be its own kind of humility. Third, who gets washed. The text says Jesus knew who would betray him, and readers notice no one is skipped: Judas's feet were in that room too. Fourth, the instruction: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." And: "I have given you an example." Churches take that in different ways. Some, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican among them, wash feet in a service on the Thursday before Easter; some smaller churches do it whenever they share communion; others read it as a picture of everyday service rather than a rite. The gesture at the center stays the same: love that kneels down.
screen: `A SERVANT'S JOB.` · `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.` · `NO ONE IS SKIPPED.` · `I HAVE GIVEN YOU AN EXAMPLE.` · then, large: `WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Look down at your own feet for a moment, then let a person come to mind whom you could serve in a small, low, unglamorous way: the dishes no one wants, the heavy bag, the boring shift. Picture yourself doing it without announcing it. Then notice whether there's someone you've refused to let serve you, and if you pray, bring both to God in a few plain words.
Washing feet. In John's Gospel, Jesus takes a servant's job at his last supper and tells his friends to do the same for one another. Today's word.
Your line: wash feet. Love that kneels, and lets itself be served. That's day eight hundred thirty-two.

833.title: No greater love
833.hook: greater love hath no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends
833.howItsDone: Christian tradition reads John 15:13 as Jesus describing his own death, and the verse is read at some funerals and carved on some memorials to people who died for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was washing feet, love that kneels down. Your line was wash feet. Today, the same night, a little later, and the week's last day.

The feet are washed. The basin is put away. In John's Gospel, Jesus keeps talking to his friends late into that last evening, and it reads like someone saying everything that matters before a door closes. Somewhere in that long talk comes one sentence about love. It sets a bar, and it's high. And in the next breath, it changes what the friends are called.
screen: `THE BASIN IS PUT AWAY.` → `A LONG TALK BEFORE A DOOR CLOSES.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETS THE BAR.`

segments.voice: First, the command it explains: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you." Not as much as you can manage. As I have loved you. Second, the sentence itself: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." In John's story it's said the night before the crucifixion, and Christian tradition hears it pointing straight at the next day: he is describing what he's about to do. Third, the word friends. A moment later: "Henceforth I call you not servants," but "I have called you friends." The Greek is a form of philos, the friend-love from earlier this block. The men whose feet he washed like a servant, he now calls friends; the rank goes the other way from what the room expected. Fourth, the small version. Dying for a friend is not a request that comes to everyone, and some readers hear a quieter meaning: a life can be laid down an hour at a time. A night shift at a sickbed. A weekend given up. A plan let go so a friend can have theirs. And the week of love's voices: clinging, holding on, the friend, seal, First John, even them, wash feet, and now lay it down. Ruth stayed, Jonathan stepped aside, the Song set love against death, John made it the test, and Jesus took the towel and named the bar.
screen: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.` · `NOT SERVANTS: FRIENDS.` · `AN HOUR AT A TIME.` · then, large: `NO GREATER LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one friend who could use something from you this week, and look at what you were planning to keep for yourself: an evening, a little money, the last word in an argument, the favor you've been saving. Pick one small thing you could set down for them, hold the picture of handing it over, and notice the little cost; that cost is the point. If you pray, you can offer it with their name.
Philos. The friend-love Jesus uses when he calls his followers friends instead of servants, the night he spoke of laying down a life for them. Today's word.
Your line: lay it down. An hour at a time counts too. A week of love's voices, done.
